question: In the ResNet paper's ImageNet comparison of 18-layer and 34-layer networks, how did the plain and residual versions differ, and why do the authors argue the plain network's problem is not caused by vanishing gradients?
reference_answer: The 34-layer plain net had higher error than the 18-layer plain net (top-1 validation error 28.54% vs 27.94%, Table 2) and higher training error throughout training; the authors call this the degradation problem. With identity shortcuts (zero-padded, so no extra parameters) the order reversed: the 34-layer ResNet reached 25.03% vs 27.88% for the 18-layer ResNet (2.8 points better). The authors argue the plain-net difficulty is unlikely to be vanishing gradients because the plain nets are trained with batch normalization, which keeps forward signals at non-zero variance, and they verified that backward gradients have healthy norms; they only conjecture that deep plain nets may have exponentially low convergence rates. Training 3x longer still showed degradation.
notes: Retrieval challenge: the Table 2 numbers are separated from the prose that explains them (pages 4-5). Numbers are top-1 validation error with 10-crop testing; the paper does not claim to have identified the true cause of degradation ('will be studied in the future'). [General-knowledge risk: medium.]

candidates.label: A
candidates.answer:
## Difference between plain and residual 18/34-layer networks

The plain and residual networks were built to have **identical architecture, depth, width, and parameter count** — the only difference is the addition of shortcut connections:

- "The baseline architectures are the same as the above plain nets, except that a shortcut connection is added to each pair of 3×3 filters as in Fig. 3 (right)." [ResNet, p.5]
- For the first comparison, identity mapping was used for all shortcuts and zero-padding for increasing dimensions (option A), "So they have no extra parameter compared to the plain counterparts." [ResNet, p.5]

**Performance difference (Table 2, top-1 error, 10-crop testing):**
| | plain | ResNet |
|---|---|---|
| 18 layers | 27.94 | 27.88 |
| 34 layers | 28.54 | 25.03 |

[ResNet, p.5]

Key observations:
- The 34-layer **plain** net has *higher* training error than the 18-layer plain net throughout training, despite the 18-layer solution space being a subspace of the 34-layer one — i.e., deeper plain net degrades. [ResNet, p.5]
- With residual connections, "the situation is reversed... the 34-layer ResNet is better than the 18-layer ResNet (by 2.8%)," and it "exhibits considerably lower training error and is generalizable to the validation data." [ResNet, p.5-6]
- Comparing the 34-layer plain net to its ResNet counterpart: the ResNet "reduces the top-1 error by 3.5%," resulting from "successfully reduced training error." [ResNet, p.6]
- For 18 layers, plain and residual nets are "comparably accurate," but the 18-layer ResNet "converges faster," easing optimization "by providing faster convergence at the early stage" when the net is "not overly deep." [ResNet, p.6]

## Why the authors argue it's not vanishing gradients

The authors give three pieces of evidence [ResNet, p.5]:

1. **BN ensures healthy signal propagation**: "These plain networks are trained with BN [16], which ensures forward propagated signals to have non-zero variances. We also verify that the backward propagated gradients exhibit healthy norms with BN. So neither forward nor backward signals vanish."

2. **The 34-layer plain net still achieves competitive accuracy** (Table 3), "suggesting that the solver works to some extent" — i.e., it's not completely failing to learn, which would be expected if gradients had vanished.

3. **More training iterations don't fix it**: In a footnote, "We have experimented with more training iterations (3×) and still observed the degradation problem, suggesting that this problem cannot be feasibly addressed by simply using more iterations." [ResNet, p.5]

Instead, they **conjecture** that "the deep plain nets may have exponentially low convergence rates, which impact the reducing of the training error," explicitly noting "The reason for such optimization difficulties will be studied in the future." [ResNet, p.5]

candidates.label: B
candidates.answer:
## How the plain and residual 18/34-layer networks differed on ImageNet

**Plain networks:** The deeper 34-layer plain net had *higher* validation error than the shallower 18-layer plain net (28.54% vs. 27.94% top-1 error, 10-crop testing), and training error curves showed the 34-layer plain net had higher training error throughout the whole training procedure, "even though the solution space of the 18-layer plain network is a subspace of that of the 34-layer one" [ResNet, p.5]. This is the degradation problem.

**Residual networks:** The situation is reversed — the 34-layer ResNet is *better* than the 18-layer ResNet by 2.8% (top-1 error), and "the 34-layer ResNet exhibits considerably lower training error and is generalizable to the validation data" [ResNet, p.5]. From Table 2: plain-18 = 27.94%, ResNet-18 = 27.88%; plain-34 = 28.54%, ResNet-34 = 25.03% [ResNet, p.5]. So adding depth hurt the plain net but helped the ResNet. In addition, "compared to its plain counterpart, the 34-layer ResNet reduces the top-1 error by 3.5%" [ResNet, p.5-6], and even at 18 layers (where plain and residual nets were comparably accurate), the 18-layer ResNet converged faster than the 18-layer plain net [ResNet, p.6].

## Why the authors say the plain net's problem is not vanishing gradients

The authors argue: "We argue that this optimization difficulty is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients. These plain networks are trained with BN [16], which ensures forward propagated signals to have non-zero variances. We also verify that the backward propagated gradients exhibit healthy norms with BN. So neither forward nor backward signals vanish." [ResNet, p.5]

They further support this by noting that "the 34-layer plain net is still able to achieve competitive accuracy (Table 3), suggesting that the solver works to some extent" [ResNet, p.5] — i.e., it isn't failing outright as a vanishing-gradient collapse would suggest. Instead, "we conjecture that the deep plain nets may have exponentially low convergence rates, which impact the reducing of the training error" [ResNet, p.5]. They also note this is checked against simply needing more training time: "We have experimented with more training iterations (3×) and still observed the degradation problem, suggesting that this problem cannot be feasibly addressed by simply using more iterations" [ResNet, footnote 3, p.5]. The paper explicitly states the actual cause is left open: "The reason for such optimization difficulties will be studied in the future" [ResNet, p.5].

question: Distillation and BYOL both train one network to match another network's outputs. According to the two papers, what supplies the targets in each case and how does that target model come about, are labels used, and what does BYOL say about the 'mean teacher' method that it treats as closest to its slow-moving-average target?
reference_answer: Distillation: the targets are class probabilities from an already-trained 'cumbersome' model (an ensemble, or a single very large model trained with a strong regularizer such as dropout), softened by raising the softmax temperature. The small model is trained at the same high temperature on a transfer set and uses temperature 1 afterwards; when labels are known the objective is a weighted average of cross-entropy with the soft targets and with the correct labels, with a considerably lower weight on the label term. BYOL: the targets are the projections a target network produces for a second augmented view; the target's weights are an exponential moving average of the online network's weights (a slow-moving average of the learner itself, not a separately trained larger model), the loss gradient is not propagated into the target (stop-gradient), and an extra predictor sits only on the online branch. BYOL is a self-supervised method that works without negative pairs. BYOL describes mean teacher (MT) as also using a slow-moving-average 'teacher' to produce targets for an online 'student', with an l2 consistency loss between their softmax predictions added to a classification loss; it reports that a similar approach collapses when the classification loss is removed, whereas BYOL's added predictor prevents collapse.
notes: Conceptual cross-paper link built from each paper's own description: the distillation paper never mentions self-supervised methods, and BYOL uses 'teacher/student' wording only for mean teacher. Do not claim that BYOL 'is' distillation; the targets differ (a fixed, already-trained larger model versus a moving average of the learner). BYOL results are on ImageNet, distillation results on MNIST, speech and JFT, so no performance comparison is implied. [General-knowledge risk: medium.]

candidates.label: A
candidates.answer:
## Source of targets in each method

**Distillation:** The targets are the soft output probabilities (soft target distribution) produced by a large, already-trained "cumbersome model" — either a single large highly regularized model or an ensemble of models — run at a high softmax temperature. "In the simplest form of distillation, knowledge is transferred to the distilled model by training it on a transfer set and using a soft target distribution for each case in the transfer set that is produced by using the cumbersome model with a high temperature in its softmax" [Distillation, p.3, Abstract]. This cumbersome/teacher model is trained separately and beforehand (e.g., as an ensemble of 10 models trained on hard labels), and its outputs are then transferred to the smaller distilled model: "our distillation approach is able to extract more useful information from the training set than simply using the hard labels to train a single model... the improvement in WER achieved by the ensemble is transferred to the distilled model" [Distillation, p.5]. So here hard labels ARE used — but to train the teacher model first; the student is then trained primarily on the teacher's soft targets (optionally combined with hard labels, as temperature reverts to 1 at deployment and training uses the high-temperature soft targets) [Distillation, p.3, Abstract; p.5].

**BYOL:** The targets come from a **target network** that has the identical architecture to the online network but a different set of weights ξ, which are not learned by gradient descent but are an **exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network's own weights θ**: "its parameters ξ are an exponential moving average of the online parameters θ" [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1]. No separate pre-trained model and no labels are used to produce these targets — they are "bootstrapped" from the network's own evolving representation: "we propose to directly bootstrap the representations... BYOL trains its online network to predict the target network's representation of another augmented view of the same image" [BYOL, p.2, Abstract]. The whole training pipeline is label-free (self-supervised); BYOL is only evaluated afterward using labels in the linear-evaluation/semi-supervised protocols [BYOL, p.2, Abstract], but the target-generation process itself uses no labels.

## BYOL's comparison to Mean Teacher

BYOL explicitly identifies Mean Teacher (MT) as the closest existing approach using a slow-moving average target network, but highlights two key differences:

1. **Mean Teacher is semi-supervised and uses labels; BYOL does not.** "In the semi-supervised setting..., an unsupervised loss is combined with a classification loss over a handful of labels... mean teacher (MT) also uses a slow-moving average network, called teacher, to produce targets for an online network, called student. An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss" [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

2. **Without the classification loss, the MT-style approach collapses, whereas BYOL does not — because of BYOL's added predictor.** "While [20] demonstrates the effectiveness of MT in the semi-supervised learning case, in Section 5 we show that a similar approach collapses when removing the classification loss. In contrast, BYOL introduces an additional predictor on top of the online network, which prevents collapse" [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

This is reiterated later: "Removing the predictor in BYOL results in an unsupervised version of MT with no classification loss that" [collapses, continuing the ablation discussion] [BYOL, p.9, section 5]. Also note a structural difference: MT's consistency loss is computed directly on softmax/logit outputs of student vs. teacher [BYOL, p.3, section 2], whereas BYOL's online network has an extra predictor stage (fθ → gθ → qθ) beyond what the target network computes (fξ → gξ only) [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1], and BYOL's loss operates on projected representations rather than classification logits.

**Summary:** Distillation's targets come from an externally, separately pre-trained (and possibly label-trained) cumbersome teacher model's soft softmax outputs at high temperature [Distillation, p.3, p.5]. BYOL's targets come from an EMA of the online network's own weights, requiring no separate teacher and no labels [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1; p.2, Abstract]. BYOL treats Mean Teacher as the closest prior slow-moving-average-target method, but notes MT requires a classification loss on labels and collapses without it, whereas BYOL avoids collapse via its predictor and remains fully unsupervised [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

candidates.label: B
candidates.answer:
# How targets are supplied in Distillation vs. BYOL

## Distillation (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean)

The targets come from a **separately, fully-trained "cumbersome model"** — either a large ensemble of models or a single large heavily-regularized model — trained *before* distillation begins:

- "The cumbersome model could be an ensemble of separately trained models or a single very large model trained with a very strong regularizer such as dropout" [Distillation, p.1].
- The target model is trained normally, typically with **hard labels**, to maximize average log probability of the correct class. The targets used for the small model are the **soft class probabilities** this trained model produces, obtained by raising the softmax temperature: "knowledge is transferred to the distilled model by training it on a transfer set and using a soft target distribution for each case in the transfer set that is produced by using the cumbersome model with a high temperature in its softmax" [Distillation, p.3].
- Labels are optionally reintroduced during the transfer step itself: "When the correct labels are known for all or some of the transfer set, this method can be significantly improved by also training the distilled model to produce the correct labels," via a weighted average of a soft-target cross-entropy loss and a hard-target cross-entropy loss [Distillation, p.3].
- In the ensemble case, the soft targets can be the "arithmetic or geometric mean" of the individual trained models' predictive distributions [Distillation, p.2].

So: targets = outputs of an **independently pre-trained** (label-supervised) model/ensemble, used post-hoc; the target model does not change during distillation.

## BYOL (Grill et al.)

The targets come from a **target network that is itself a continuously-updated exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network being trained** — not a separately pretrained model:

- "The target network provides the regression targets to train the online network, and its parameters ξ are an exponential moving average of the online parameters θ... ξ ← τξ + (1−τ)θ" [BYOL, p.3].
- No labels are used at all: BYOL is self-supervised — the online network predicts the target network's projection of a *different augmented view of the same (unlabeled) image* [BYOL, p.3–4]. Labels appear only later in optional linear-evaluation/semi-supervised fine-tuning, not in producing the targets.
- The target network co-evolves with the online network during training (it is not a fixed, finished model); only the online encoder is kept at the end [BYOL, p.3–4].

## BYOL's discussion of Mean Teacher (its closest comparison for the slow-moving-average target)

BYOL explicitly compares itself to **Mean Teacher (MT)**, the semi-supervised method it treats as closest to its own target-network mechanism:

- "Mean teacher (MT) [20] also uses a slow-moving average network, called teacher, to produce targets for an online network, called student. An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss." [BYOL, p.3]
- Key difference: MT relies on **a classification loss over labels** to "ground the training" of its EMA target. BYOL shows that removing this classification loss (making MT's mechanism fully unsupervised) causes collapse: "[20] demonstrates the effectiveness of MT in the semi-supervised learning case, in Section 5 we show that a similar approach collapses when removing the classification loss. In contrast, BYOL introduces an additional predictor on top of the online network, which prevents collapse." [BYOL, p.3]
- This is confirmed quantitatively in the ablations: "Removing the predictor in BYOL results in an unsupervised version of MT with no classification loss that uses image augmentations instead of the original architectural noise (e.g., dropout). This variant of BYOL collapses (Row 7 of Table 5) which suggests that the additional predictor is critical to prevent collapse in an unsupervised scenario." [BYOL, p.9–10]

So BYOL's argument is: MT's slow-moving-average target works because labels anchor the student via a classification loss; take the labels away and MT's approach collapses, whereas BYOL avoids collapse without labels by adding a **predictor** on the online branch — this predictor (plus the EMA target) is what BYOL identifies as the key ingredient MT lacks.

candidates.label: C
candidates.answer:
## Where the targets come from

**Distillation:** The targets are produced by a *cumbersome model*—in the reported experiment, an **ensemble of 10 models**—rather than by a self-referential copy of the student network. The paper states that "our distillation approach is able to extract more useful information from the training set than simply using the hard labels to train a single model" and that improvements the 10-model ensemble achieves (in frame classification accuracy and WER) are largely transferred to the distilled model [Distillation, p.5]. This passage contrasts two uses of labels: (1) training a single model directly on the **hard labels**, versus (2) distilling knowledge from the ensemble. The evidence given does not state whether the ensemble members themselves were trained with hard labels or whether the distilled (student) model also uses hard labels alongside the distillation targets—only that the alternative to distillation is "using the hard labels to train a single model" [Distillation, p.5]. So the passage establishes that distillation targets come from an ensemble of separately-trained models, but it does not fully specify the labeling regime for either the ensemble or the student beyond this comparison.

**BYOL:** The targets come from a **target network** that has the same architecture as the online network but a different set of weights ξ. Critically, ξ is **not independently trained**—it is an **exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network's own weights θ**, updated after every training step according to a decay rate τ ∈ [0,1] [BYOL, p.3]. This is a purely self-referential ("bootstrap") mechanism: the online network fθ/gθ/qθ is trained to predict the output of a slowly-evolving copy of itself. Nothing in the provided passages indicates that labels are used to produce these targets—the target network's weights derive entirely from the online network's own parameter history [BYOL, p.3].

## Labels

- Distillation: hard labels are referenced only as the baseline alternative to distillation ("using the hard labels to train a single model") [Distillation, p.5]; the provided passage does not describe labels being used to generate the distillation targets themselves—those come from the ensemble's outputs.
- BYOL: no labels are involved in producing the target-network outputs; the target is purely an EMA of the online network's weights [BYOL, p.3].

## BYOL on "mean teacher" (its closest slow-moving-average analogue)

An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss" [BYOL, p.3]. # Source of Targets in Distillation vs. BYOL

**What supplies the targets:** The targets are **soft targets** — class probabilities produced by a "cumbersome model" using a softened softmax: "In the simplest form of distillation, knowledge is transferred to the distilled model by training it on a transfer set and using a soft target distribution for each case in the transfer set that is produced by using the cumbersome model with a high temperature in its softmax" [Distillation, p.3].

**How the target model comes about:** The cumbersome model is typically **a separately, fully-trained ensemble** (or a single large heavily regularized model): "The cumbersome model could be an ensemble of separately trained models or a single very large model trained with a very strong regularizer such as dropout" [Distillation, p.1]. In the speech experiment, this means training "10 separate models ... using exactly the same architecture and training procedure as the baseline. The models are randomly initialized with different initial parameter values" and averaging their predictions [Distillation, p.5].

**Are labels used?** Yes, optionally, alongside the soft targets. The cumbersome/ensemble model is itself trained on labeled data in the normal way. For the small (distilled) model, "When the correct labels are known for all or some of the transfer set, this method can be significantly improved by also training the distilled model to produce the correct labels," using "a weighted average of two different objective functions" — cross-entropy with soft targets and cross-entropy with the correct hard labels [Distillation, p.3]. The transfer set "could consist entirely of unlabeled data... or we could use the original training set" [Distillation, p.2].

## BYOL (Grill et al.)

**What supplies the targets:** The **target network** produces the regression targets: "The target network provides the regression targets to train the online network" [BYOL, p.3]. Specifically, "the target network outputs y′ξ = fξ(v′) and the target projection z′ξ = gξ(y′) from the second augmented view v′" [BYOL, p.3].

**How the target model comes about:** The target network has the *same architecture* as the online network but different weights ξ, which are **an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network's weights θ** (not a separately trained model and not a fixed copy): "its parameters ξ are an exponential moving average of the online parameters θ... given a target decay rate τ ∈ [0,1], after each training step we perform the following update, ξ ← τξ + (1−τ)θ" [BYOL, p.3].

**Are labels used?** No — BYOL is self-supervised; the targets come purely from a differently-augmented view of the same unlabeled image, with no class labels involved in generating the targets [BYOL, p.3-4].

## BYOL's discussion of Mean Teacher (the method it treats as closest to its EMA target)

BYOL explicitly compares itself to **Mean Teacher (MT)** as the closest prior use of a slow-moving-average target:

- "Among these methods, mean teacher (MT) [20] also uses a slow-moving average network, called teacher, to produce targets for an online network, called student. An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss" [BYOL, p.3].
- Key difference: MT is **semi-supervised** — it combines the consistency loss with a classification loss on labels. BYOL notes: "While [20] demonstrates the effectiveness of MT in the semi-supervised learning case, in Section 5 we show that a similar approach **collapses when removing the classification loss**. In contrast, BYOL introduces an additional predictor on top of the online network, which prevents collapse" [BYOL, p.3].
- This is confirmed experimentally: "Removing the predictor in BYOL results in an unsupervised version of MT with no classification loss that uses image augmentations instead of the original architectural noise (e.g., dropout). This variant of BYOL collapses (Row 7 of Table 5) which suggests that the additional predictor is critical to prevent collapse in an unsupervised scenario" [BYOL, p.9-10].

So BYOL's stated distinction from Mean Teacher is: MT relies on labels (a classification loss) to avoid collapse, whereas BYOL has no labels and instead relies on an added **predictor network** on the online branch to prevent the representation from collapsing to a trivial constant.
